title: Record Heatwave Kills Three Lions in Tokyo as East Asia Swelters
summary: Lions evolved on the scorching plains of Africa, but they're no match for Japan's deadly combination of heat and humidity. In a grim milestone, three lionesses at Tokyo's Tama Zoological Park — Mugi (3), Ichigo (11), and Luena (15) — died within a week from suspected heatstroke. 'Even though lions are thought to be resistant to heat, zookeepers have been strengthening countermeasures,' a zoo spokeswoman said. 'Heat here comes with high humidity that is different from heat with dry air in Africa.' The deaths underscore a brutal reality: East Asia is baking under a record-shattering heatwave that's straining health systems and claiming lives. South Korea's temperature hit 42.5°C (108.5°F) in Yangsan on Sunday — the highest in 122 years of observations — prompting President Lee to declare a national disaster. The death toll has reached 19, with 13 victims aged 80 or above, and over 2,000 heat-related illnesses reported since May. 'An even greater concern is that abnormal weather conditions make it highly likely that extreme weather will continue,' Lee warned, calling for a redesign of disaster response. In Japan, nearly 18,600 people were hospitalized for heatstroke in a single week, with 45 dead on arrival. Parts of the country have hit 40°C, earning the new designation 'cruelly hot day.' North Korea's state media showed crowded water parks but offered no casualty figures — a reminder of the information blackout there. Scientists attribute the crisis to human-driven climate change, which makes heatwaves more frequent and intense. The UN weather agency also flagged a strengthening El Niño, a natural climate pattern that typically amplifies global temperatures and disrupts rainfall. Europe is battling wildfires, and the U.S. faces elevated fire risks. For the lions of Tama Zoo, the tragedy is a stark symbol: in a rapidly warming world, even the king of beasts can fall victim to the heat.
why_it_matters: The deaths of these lionesses are a chilling symbol of a planet in crisis. For young people, this heatwave is not an anomaly; it's a preview of summers to come, and it signals that wildlife, human health, and even the stability of entire countries are at stake unless climate action accelerates.

background_read: Tama Zoological Park, a large zoo in western Tokyo, is home to many species, but even animals considered heat-tolerant can succumb when humidity prevents evaporative cooling—a problem not encountered on the dry African plains. The lion deaths are part of a broader pattern: extreme heat now kills more people globally than hurricanes or floods, and events like the 2003 European heatwave (which caused 70,000 deaths) or the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome show how unprepared many regions are.

El Niño, a natural warming of the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, tends to push up planetary temperatures. The World Meteorological Organization (the UN agency that monitors global climate) warned that the latest El Niño is supercharging an already warm baseline created by decades of greenhouse gas emissions.

North Korea's state media showed happy scenes at water parks but released no casualty figures—a reminder that not all governments publicly track heat-related deaths, leaving vulnerable populations invisible in global statistics.

perspectives.description: The tragedy could push zoos and cities to adopt better cooling technologies and emergency protocols. It also raises public awareness, potentially building support for green infrastructure and heat action plans that save human lives as well.

Even wealthy nations like Japan and South Korea were overwhelmed, revealing a dangerous lack of readiness. The lack of data from North Korea raises fears that many elderly and poor people are dying uncounted, a stark example of how inequality worsens climate impacts.

Climate scientists have long warned that a major El Niño year on top of background warming would produce extreme heat events. This heatwave fits that model perfectly, illustrating how natural variability now interacts with a human-altered climate system.

As heat of this intensity becomes more common, societies will have to redesign everything from building codes to school schedules. Investment in early warning systems and climate-resilient infrastructure could become as routine as earthquake preparedness in Japan.
